citation.title: Composite 3D-printed Plate-based Mechanical Metamaterials
citation.authors: Aya Hosoi, Jier Wang, Yuki Fujita, Tatsuo Tanaka, Junichi Takahashi, Ajit Panesar
citation.venue: 24th International Conference on Composite Materials (ICCM-24), Baltimore, USA, 4-8 August 2025 (conference paper, deposited on Zenodo)
citation.version_coded: Full text (9 pages, file ICCM24_Final_Paper_054.pdf), CC BY-SA 4.0, downloaded from the Zenodo record. doi.org and zenodo.org/doi/... returned a 403 'unusual traffic' rate-limit page to a generic-UA curl request (a bot/rate-limit check, not bypassed); WebFetch reached the record page and, on a second call to the exact file URL shown on that page, retrieved the actual PDF binary, which was extracted with PyMuPDF.

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: Not coded (excluded). Headline: a two-step pipeline -- (1) classical density-based low-resolution topology optimisation of a macro-scale MBB-beam problem, giving a per-element target elastic tensor and volume fraction, then (2) a pretrained multi-layer-perceptron inverse generator mapping that target tensor to 2D or 3D (truss- or plate-based BCC) lattice unit-cell parameters -- produces 'optimal' lattice structures for orthotropic (fibre-reinforced Onyx) and isotropic (Nylon) materials. FEA of a three-point-bending test (Tables 3-5) shows these optimal structures have lower compliance / higher specific stiffness than non-optimised 'uniform' counterpart lattices of the same cell count, and that 3D plate-based BCC outperforms truss-based BCC (specific stiffness 671.4 vs 143.9).
claim.location: Abstract; Sec. 3 (Results and Discussions), Tables 3-5; Sec. 4 (Conclusions)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Not coded (excluded at full text). No runtime, iteration count, or computational-cost figure is reported for any method (classical or ML) anywhere in the article; efficiency is asserted only as a generic, uncited motivation in the Introduction ('optimisation leveraging machine learning... has gained interest as a computationally efficient approach [8]', citing an external review, not this article's own measurement).

notes: Excluded under PROTOCOL §4 and the 2026-09-24 FT-NOBASELINE clarification: every quantitative comparison in the article (Tables 3, 4, 5) is between the proposed method's own output ('Optimal', produced by the classical-TO-plus-MLP pipeline) and a non-optimised 'Uniform (benchmark)' lattice of the same cell count and material -- i.e. optimisation vs. no optimisation, not the proposed (TO+ML) method vs. an alternative classical, non-learned optimisation method (e.g. dehomogenization or inverse homogenisation run without the ML step, which the Introduction cites [5], [6], [7] only as background). The article never runs, times, or reports a result for any such classical comparator, so it does not meet PROTOCOL §3.2/§4's comparison requirement even though it clearly is TO/architected-material inverse design in scope (§3.1) and clearly uses a learned model (an MLP inverse generator, trained on 5000 randomly generated unit-cell samples, Sec. 2.1.2) for what is genuinely an optimisation-level task (inverse design of unit-cell geometry from a target elastic tensor), not mere forward prediction -- so FT-SCOPE, FT-DOMAIN, FT-NOML and FT-FORWARD (the higher-priority codes) do not apply, and FT-MLONLY does not fit either since the comparator is a non-method baseline, not another ML method. This judgment rests on a full reading of the 9-page conference paper, not an inference from the abstract alone. No author named Jun Wang: co-author 'Jier Wang' is a different given name (not 'Jun'), and 'Junichi Takahashi' has 'Jun' only as part of a different personal name with a different surname; neither is a match.
